learn.title: The two cases
learn.body: A recursive function has a base case, an input answered without calling itself, and a recursive case, which calls itself on something smaller. The base case is what makes it stop.

learn.title: Sum of 1 to n
learn.body: Base case: the sum of 1 to 1 is just 1. Recursive case: n plus the sum of 1 to n - 1.

learn.title: Expanding sum(3)
learn.body: The calls go down to the base case, then the answers come back up.
steps: `sum(1)` hits the base case and returns 1

learn.title: Why a missing base case is a bug
learn.body: Each call that is waiting uses a little memory, called a stack frame. Without a base case the calls never stop, memory runs out and the program usually crashes with a stack overflow. The exact message depends on the system.

learn.title: Each call must get closer
learn.body: The recursive case must move toward the base case. If `sum` called `sum(n)` or `sum(n + 1)`, it would never reach 1. Always check two things: there is a base case, and every call heads toward it.

questions.prompt: What is the base case in `sum`?
questions.explanation: For n of 1 the answer is known directly without recursion.
It is the base case, which returns 1 at once.

questions.prompt: A recursive function with no \_\_ never stops calling itself.
questions.explanation: The base case is the only thing that ends the chain of calls.

questions.prompt: What usually happens when recursion has no base case?
choices: The program crashes from a stack overflow
The compiler refuses to build it
questions.explanation: Memory for the waiting calls runs out. The compiler can not tell, so it still builds.

questions.prompt: Why would `return n + sum(n);` be wrong?
questions.explanation: Each call would make the same call again, never moving to the base case.

questions.prompt: Put the evaluation of `sum(3)` in order.
questions.explanation: Calls go down to the base case, and the results return back up.
